query: For an equimolar WTaTiVZr high-entropy alloy made from low-activation refractory elements, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains its plastic strain and toughness relative to commercially used pure tungsten under high-temperature mechanical loading relevant to sustained plasma-facing-component service? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the hypothesized cause, the observations expected relative to pure tungsten, the applicable boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The equimolar WTaTiVZr high‐entropy alloy exhibits superior plastic strain and toughness at high temperatures compared to pure tungsten because its severe lattice distortion produces a nanocrystalline, heavily distorted BCC microstructure. This microstructure is predisposed to activate grain boundary–mediated plasticity (e.g., grain boundary sliding), rather than relying exclusively on dislocation slip, thereby delaying void formation and crack propagation under high-temperature service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: WTaTiVZr alloy fabricated as an equimolar composition with a nanocrystalline, severely distorted BCC structure versus commercially pure tungsten with a coarse-grained, dislocation‐dominated BCC structure.
generation.intervention: Subject both the WTaTiVZr alloy and pure tungsten to identical high-temperature (e.g., around 1000°C) mechanical loading tests (compression or tensile) at controlled strain rates.
generation.conditions: High-temperature regimes (800–1100°C) under inert atmosphere, with identical strain rates and load histories representative of plasma-facing-component conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanostructured BCC matrix with a high density of grain boundaries resulting from severe lattice distortions inherent to the equimolar refractory high-entropy alloy.
generation.mechanism: The severe lattice distortion in the alloy increases its grain boundary area and disrupts classical dislocation slip, promoting grain boundary sliding and intergranular plastic flow. This mechanism enables more uniform deformation and energy absorption, delaying crack initiation compared to pure tungsten which deforms primarily by dislocation slip leading to brittle, cleavage-dominated failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-temperature mechanical loading, the WTaTiVZr alloy will exhibit a lower yield stress but much higher total plastic strain and fracture toughness compared to pure tungsten. Fractographic and microstructural analyses will reveal intergranular features and evidence of grain-boundary sliding in the alloy, in contrast to the cleavage fractures and limited plasticity observed in tungsten.
generation.baseline: Pure tungsten subjected to the same high-temperature mechanical tests is expected to deform predominantly by dislocation slip and show minimal plastic strain with brittle fracture.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective under high-temperature conditions (800–1100°C) relevant to plasma-facing applications; at lower temperatures or under different loading modes the deformation mechanism may revert to predominantly dislocation-mediated plasticity.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in ductility and toughness and the extent of grain-boundary sliding are influenced by processing history (grain size distribution, residual stresses) and require further experimental quantification.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate samples of the equimolar WTaTiVZr alloy and commercially pure tungsten. Perform high-temperature (approximately 1000°C) mechanical tests (compression or tension) under identical strain rates. Follow up with detailed microstructural characterization (using TEM, EBSD, and fractography) to assess deformation mechanisms.
measurements: Yield strength, total plastic strain, and fracture toughness
Fracture surface analysis to identify intergranular slipping versus cleavage
TEM evaluation of grain boundary sliding or other intergranular deformation features
Comparison of dislocation density and grain size changes pre- and post-deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If under identical high-temperature loading conditions the WTaTiVZr alloy does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in plastic strain and toughness compared to pure tungsten, or if both materials show similar (dislocation-dominated) deformation mechanisms without evidence of grain boundary sliding, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Question: Can a quaternary tungsten-based refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) exhibit superior radiation resistance compared to pure tungsten, specifically regarding the formation of dislocation loops under fusion-relevant irradiation conditions?. System: Quaternary W-Ta-V-Cr high-entropy alloy with atomic composition 38% W, 36% Ta, 15% Cr, and 11% V. Processing: Magnetron sputtering deposition from pure metal targets (99.99% purity) using powers of 192 W (Cr), 312 W (V), 277 W (Ta), and 300 W (W) at 3 mtorr pressure and room temperature; films deposited on NaCl (100 nm) or Si (3 μm) substrates. Question: How can a nanocrystalline refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film with superior mechanical and tribological properties be synthesized using a cost-effective single target, and what are the effects of annealing on its adhesion and wear performance?. System: Equimolar CuMoTaWV refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates. Processing: DC-magnetron sputtering using a single target prepared by partial spark plasma sintering (SPS) of equimolar elemental powders (Cu, Mo, Ta, W, V) at 1000 °C under 40 MPa pressure; film deposition at 500 °C substrate temperature for 120 min in Ar atmosphere (1.16 × 10⁻³ mPa, 150 W power); post-deposition annealing at 300 °C for adhesion improvement. Test conditions: Nanoindentation at 3 mN load; nanopillar compression (440 nm diameter, 3 mN max force); tribological wear tests at room temperature (RT) and 300 °C with 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed against E52100 alloy steel counterballs. Findings: The as-deposited film exhibited a nanocrystalline body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution with an average grain size of 18 nm and a thickness of ~900 nm.; Nanoindentation measurement
